title: Leviticus 19:30–37
context: The chapter closes with Sabbath and sanctuary, rejection of mediums, honor for the elderly, love for the foreigner, and honest weights and measures. The final reminder that the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt grounds ethics in redemption. Both traditions share this reading: grace precedes and motivates obedience, and love for the stranger reflects Israel’s own history.

verses.text: “ ‘You shall keep my Sabbaths, and reverence my sanctuary; I am the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Keep Sabbaths and reverence the sanctuary. Arminian readers see holy time and holy space honored. Worship shapes life. Sabbath and sanctuary belong together as marks of a people devoted to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see reverence for God’s presence. Views on Sabbath vary within both traditions. The reverence is shared. The command also echoes verse 3, framing the chapter with worship.

verses.text: “ ‘Don’t turn to those who are mediums, nor to the wizards. Don’t seek them out, to be defiled by them. I am the LORD your God.
verses.arminianNotes: Do not turn to mediums or wizards. Arminian readers see reliance on God alone for guidance. Seeking spirits defiles. The LORD alone is Israel’s guide, and other sources of guidance lead astray.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the occult as rival worship. Both traditions share this reading. Deuteronomy 18:10–12 lists similar practices. Turning to mediums betrays trust in the LORD.

verses.text: “ ‘You shall rise up before the gray head and honor the face of the elderly; and you shall fear your God. I am the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Rise before the elderly and honor them; fear God. Arminian readers see respect for age as part of holiness. Honoring the old reflects reverence for God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see dignity given to the elderly. Both traditions share this reading. The fear of God is linked to respect for those whose age gives them honor in the community.

verses.text: “ ‘If a stranger lives as a foreigner with you in your land, you shall not do him wrong.
verses.arminianNotes: Do not wrong the foreigner. Arminian readers see protection for vulnerable outsiders. God cares for the stranger. Foreigners were especially vulnerable to mistreatment in ancient societies.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see justice extended beyond Israel. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground. Exodus 22:21 and 23:9 give the same command, grounding it in Israel’s own experience.

verses.text: The stranger who lives as a foreigner with you shall be to you as the native-born among you, and you shall love him as yourself; for you lived as foreigners in the land of Egypt. I am the LORD your God.
verses.arminianNotes: Treat the foreigner as native-born and love him as yourself, remembering Egypt. Arminian readers see neighbor love extended to outsiders. Memory of grace shapes compassion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see redemption motivating love for the stranger. Both traditions share this reading. Love for the stranger extends verse 18 beyond Israel to anyone living among them.

verses.text: “ ‘You shall do no unrighteousness in judgment, in measures of length, of weight, or of quantity.
verses.arminianNotes: Do no injustice in measures of length, weight, or quantity. Arminian readers see honesty in commerce as holiness. Fraud wrongs neighbors. God cares about fairness in ordinary trade.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s justice in everyday trade. Both traditions share this reading. Honest measures protect buyers who cannot verify what they are given, especially the poor.

verses.text: You shall have just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin. I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: Use just balances and measures, for the LORD brought you out of Egypt. Arminian readers see redemption grounding ethics. Modern equivalents for the ephah and hin are approximate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see grace preceding obedience. Both traditions share this reading. The reminder of the Exodus grounds honest trade in the God who freed Israel from oppression.

verses.text: “ ‘You shall observe all my statutes and all my ordinances, and do them. I am the LORD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Observe all God’s statutes and ordinances. Arminian readers see a closing call to wholehearted obedience. The refrain ends the chapter. Obedience is to be complete, not selective.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the law as the shape of a grateful life. Both traditions share this reading. The final refrain I am the LORD gathers the chapter’s many commands under God’s authority.
